A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LatentTSF work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original material can be matched across renumbering and relocation; v2 adds material without removing essential comparison evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on six datasets with six backbones, together with loss sensitivity, AutoEncoder, and representation analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative representation analysis, ablations, corruption tests, and encoder-budget and latent-dimension studies.

M1.justification: The point-wise AutoEncoder pre-training, frozen encoder/decoder, latent forecasting, prediction-plus-cosine-alignment objective, and decoding procedure remain unchanged. Section 3.3 relaxes the feature-expansion description, but the retained architecture settings and equations do not establish an actual method change.

E1.justification: The six forecasting datasets remain unchanged. Section 5.7 and Appendix J add ETTh1 evaluation under Gaussian input noise and randomly missing inputs, extending coverage to corrupted-input scenarios.

E2.justification: The six main comparison backbones remain CMoS, DLinear, PatchTST, TimeBase, TimeXer, and iTransformer. Table 12 adds DLinear trained with alignment directly in observation space as a comparator; v1's latent-loss sweeps did not include this comparison.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs introduce CKA, effective rank, and temporal transition consistency; Gaussian noise levels of 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5; missing rates up to 30%; encoder budgets of 50–500 epochs; and Traffic latent dimensions of 512 and 862. The original splits, forecasting horizons, and main hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 5.5–5.7 and Appendices G–K substantially expand the analyses: separating latent prediction from observation-space alignment, measuring latent structure, testing encoder-budget sensitivity, evaluating input corruption, and sweeping latent dimension. The original loss-weight, AutoEncoder fine-tuning, and visualization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's variation across encoder budgets measures sensitivity to settings, rather than statistical uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: All nine original tables retain their numerical contents, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3 and 11–15. For example, Table 14 reports ETTh1 PatchTST MSE of 0.5044 versus 0.4761 with LatentTSF at 30% missingness. These are newly reported comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains; several new full-model scores differ from the retained main results without sufficiently explained setting differences.

T1.justification: v2 adds norm- and Lipschitz-based definitions in Appendix A and a frozen-encoder anti-collapse argument in Remark 3.1 and Appendix C.3. Section 4.2 also explicitly acknowledges that removing negative-sample normalization breaks the InfoNCE bound. These additions extend and qualify the theoretical justification, while the earlier derivations largely remain.

C1.justification: The central contributions—identifying Latent Chaos and forecasting through learned latent states—remain. The abstract and conclusion qualify mutual-information maximization as surrogate motivation, the abstract removes mandatory dimensional expansion, and the conclusion adds an explicit claim that the frozen encoder structurally excludes collapse.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about the relative contributions of latent prediction and alignment, encoder quality, corruption robustness, and dimensionality. Appendix A distinguishes coherence from simple smoothness, and Appendix L introduces limitations concerning the unstructured operator, frozen encoder, and non-rigorous MI surrogate. Some new blanket interpretations are contradicted by Tables 12–13.

D1.justification: Appendices I and K provide explicit encoder pre-training budgets and disclose that Traffic dimensions above 862 exceeded GPU memory. The main implementation settings, hardware specification, and code-access information remain unchanged; the new budget information concerns the added sensitivity study.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including DBLoss, DUET, PHAT, and TFB, removes WPMixer and the latent-diffusion reference, and expands the comparison with SimSiam/BYOL around frozen targets. The overall research positioning remains similar. Publication-year and venue updates for existing works do not constitute new comparisons.

P1.justification: The abstract, dimensionality explanation, and theoretical framing receive targeted edits. New analytical subsections, definitions, limitations, and acknowledgements expand the structure, while the original narrative and most wording remain. Existing sections and appendices are renumbered rather than substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially with representation metrics, decoupling, encoder-budget, corruption, and dimension-sweep tables. Tables 3 and 11 display the same new metrics twice. Existing table captions move above their tables, Figure 2's caption is clarified, and material is reflowed; all eight original figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The added corruption tests and representation metrics address evidential gaps in v1, while the explicit MI-bound caveat and limitations improve qualification. However, Table 12 contradicts its claimed universal ranking: observation-space alignment beats latent prediction alone on ETTm1 and ETTm2. Table 13 contradicts the claim that every encoder budget beats the baseline: Electricity at 300 epochs gives 0.2071 versus 0.2006. The new anti-collapse argument also assumes exact target reproduction without establishing its feasibility from historical inputs. These benefits and new reliability problems leave the net quality direction uncertain.
